Sheffield.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of South Yorkshire
s1loc: Sheffield draws millions of visits a year to a city-centre cluster led by the Millennium Gallery with its Ruskin and Metalwork Collections, the Kelham Island Museum with the River Don Engine, the most powerful working steam engine in Europe, and Weston Park Museum. Sheffield Cathedral, Bramall Lane and the Hillsborough stadium tours add to the draw, with the Steel City heritage story keeping these named landmarks busy throughout the visitor season.

The leisure and activity layer is broad, from the Winter Garden glasshouse and the Peace Gardens to Sheffield Botanical Gardens, Endcliffe Park and the Porter Valley walk. Magna Science Adventure Centre and Rother Valley Country Park sit close by, the Peak District opens on the doorstep for walkers and climbers, and Meadowhall and Ponds Forge keep family attractions and activity operators working hard across every season of the year.

Heritage and culture run deep, from the Abbeydale Industrial Hamlet and Shepherd Wheel to the Graves Gallery, the Cathedral and the Cultural Industries Quarter. The Crucible, Lyceum and Library theatres on Tudor Square, the Utilita Arena, and the Tramlines festival give event teams and venue crews a full calendar, with Kelham Island, Nether Edge and the Devonshire Quarter drawing weekend crowds into the city.

Underpinning it all is a deep hotel trade across the city centre and Ecclesall Road and a busy tour-operator and walking-guide scene. Sheffield station and the Supertram feed visitors in from across the region, while the Peak District National Park, Chatsworth and the surrounding Pennine villages give day-trippers a strong seasonal draw that keeps the wider South Yorkshire visitor trade moving through spring, summer and the festive months.

Manchester.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of Greater Manchester
s1loc: Manchester runs one of the UK's largest visitor economies, with the Science and Industry Museum on the site of the world's oldest surviving passenger railway station, the Manchester Museum, the Whitworth and the People's History Museum among the marquee draws. Old Trafford and the Etihad Stadium both run popular tours, while the National Football Museum and Manchester Cathedral pull steady visitor numbers into the city centre throughout the year.

The leisure and activity layer is huge. Heaton Park, one of Europe's largest municipal parks, the Chill Factore indoor ski slope and the Trafford Centre anchor family days out, while Manchester Aquatics Centre and the National Cycling Centre draw activity groups. Boat trips along the Bridgewater Canal at Castlefield and the Manchester Christmas Markets keep family attractions and event teams working hard across every season of the visitor year.

Heritage and culture run deep, from the Roman fort and warehouses of the Castlefield basin to the Northern Quarter, Ancoats and Spinningfields. The AO Arena, the Bridgewater Hall, the Palace Theatre, the Opera House, HOME and the Aviva Studios at Factory International host hundreds of shows a year, with the Manchester International Festival and a packed calendar drawing crowds into the Gay Village and Deansgate.

Underpinning it all is a deep hotel trade and a busy tour-operator and walking-guide scene. Manchester Airport, Piccadilly station and the Metrolink tram network feed visitors into named quarters across the city, while MediaCityUK at Salford Quays, the Lowry and the surrounding Pennine moors and reservoirs give day-trippers a strong seasonal draw that keeps the wider Greater Manchester visitor trade busy all year round.

Leicester.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of Leicestershire
s1loc: Leicester's visitor economy turns on the King Richard III Visitor Centre and the neighbouring Leicester Cathedral, where the king was reinterred in 2015, plus the multi-award-winning National Space Centre with its rocket tower and the UK's largest domed planetarium. The Jewry Wall Roman site, the New Walk Museum and Art Gallery and the medieval Guildhall add depth, drawing heritage and family visitors into the Old Town across the season.

The leisure and activity layer is strong. Abbey Park and Watermead Country Park sit beside the city, Bradgate Park in Charnwood Forest draws walkers to its deer herds and the ruins of Lady Jane Grey's birthplace, and Twycross Zoo lies a short drive out. King Power Stadium tours and the Highcross shopping quarter pull crowds, keeping family attractions and activity operators busy across every season of the visitor year.

Heritage and culture run deep, from the Roman and medieval city to the Lanes, St Martins and the Cultural Quarter around the Curve theatre and LCB Depot. The Curve and Haymarket theatres, the De Montfort Hall concert venue, the Diwali celebrations on the Golden Mile and the Caribbean Carnival give event teams a packed calendar, with Clarendon Park and the Golden Mile drawing steady footfall.

Underpinning it all is a solid city-centre hotel trade and a busy tour-operator and guide scene. Leicester station and the M1 corridor feed visitors in, with the National Forest, Rutland Water and Foxton Locks giving day-trippers a strong seasonal draw close by. The wider Leicestershire countryside, from Charnwood Forest to the Bosworth Battlefield, keeps the area's visitor trade moving through spring, summer and the festive season.

Bradford.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of West Yorkshire
s1loc: Bradford, UK City of Culture 2025, anchors its visitor economy on the National Science and Media Museum, home to the UK's first IMAX, and the UNESCO World Heritage village of Saltaire with Salts Mill and its David Hockney collection. Cartwright Hall in Lister Park, Bolling Hall and the City Park mirror pool add to the draw, pulling heritage and family visitors into the district across the year.

The leisure and activity layer is busy. Lister Park and Peel Park give green space in the heart of the city, the Keighley and Worth Valley Railway runs steam trains to Haworth, and the Bradford Industrial Museum at Eccleshill tells the wool-trade story. Ilkley Moor and Penistone Hill Country Park sit close by for walkers, keeping family attractions and activity operators working through every season of the visitor year.

Heritage and culture run deep, from the wool-trade Little Germany quarter and the Wool Exchange to Undercliffe Cemetery and the Bronte Parsonage at Haworth. The Alhambra Theatre, St George's Hall, the Bradford Literature Festival and a packed City of Culture programme give event teams a full calendar, with Saltaire, Little Germany and Manningham drawing steady visitor footfall throughout the year.

Underpinning it all is a growing city-centre hotel trade and a busy tour-operator and guide scene. Forster Square and the Interchange stations feed visitors in, while Bolton Abbey, the Yorkshire Dales and the Bronte moors around Haworth give day-trippers a strong seasonal draw. The wider West Yorkshire countryside keeps the district's visitor trade moving through spring, summer and the festive months across the calendar.

Coventry.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of Warwickshire
s1loc: Coventry's visitor economy turns on the ruins of the old Cathedral beside Sir Basil Spence's modernist Coventry Cathedral, and on the Coventry Transport Museum, which holds the largest publicly owned British vehicle collection and the world land-speed record cars. The Herbert Art Gallery and Museum, with Dippy the dinosaur in residence, St Mary's Guildhall and the medieval Spon Street add to the draw across the visitor year.

The leisure and activity layer is broad. The War Memorial Park and the Coventry Canal Basin give green and waterside space in the city, The Wave waterpark draws family groups, and Coombe Abbey Country Park offers 500 acres of gardens, woodland and lakeside walks just outside. The Coventry Building Society Arena and FarGo Village pull crowds, keeping activity operators and event teams busy across every season of the year.

Heritage and culture run deep, from the Lady Godiva legend and the medieval city walls to the Charterhouse and the Cathedral Quarter. The Belgrade Theatre and the Albany, the city's UK City of Culture legacy events and the Godiva Festival give event teams a full calendar, with named areas like Spon Street, FarGo Village and Earlsdon drawing steady visitor footfall throughout the year.

Underpinning it all is a solid city-centre hotel trade and a busy tour-operator and guide scene. Coventry station, the nearby Birmingham Airport and the M6 and M40 corridors feed visitors in, while Kenilworth Castle, Warwick Castle and Stratford-upon-Avon give day-trippers a strong seasonal draw close by. The wider Warwickshire countryside keeps the area's visitor trade moving through spring, summer and the festive season.
